title: The Worst Mistake A Teacher Can Make
author: Michael Linsin
summary: In this reflective piece, Michael Linsin identifies the single biggest error a caring teacher can make: making excuses for poor student behavior by blaming external circumstances such as unsupportive parents, tough neighborhoods, large class sizes, or particular difficult students. He argues that the moment a teacher begins looking outside themselves for the cause of misbehavior, they unconsciously communicate to students that they've given up, undermining their own ability to lead. Linsin contrasts this with the empowering effect of taking full responsibility for everything that happens in the classroom, which he says floods a teacher with confidence and capability. He notes that SCM receives many emails from teachers seeking validation for their excuses, and pushes back firmly, insisting that no teaching situation is beyond dramatic improvement. The article closes with an emphatic call to never give up on any student regardless of background or behavior.
points: The worst mistake a teacher can make is to excuse poor behavior by blaming outside circumstances rather than taking ownership.
Blaming external factors unconsciously signals to students that the teacher has given up on them, and students sense this even when it's not said aloud.
Taking full responsibility for classroom outcomes is described as deeply empowering, generating confidence and leadership ability.
Common excuses cited by struggling teachers—difficult parents, tough neighborhoods, large class sizes, challenging individual students—are real but not insurmountable barriers.
Linsin insists every student can learn, behave, and love school, and the teacher's job is to show them how, regardless of circumstances.
quotes: You see, the worst mistake you can make as a (caring) teacher is to make excuses for poor behavior.
Because as soon as you do, as soon as you start looking outside yourself for why your students are the way they are, you undermine your ability to do anything about it.
Taking responsibility for everything that happens in your classroom, on the other hand, is deeply empowering.
No doubt these factors exist, but they’re not insurmountable—not even close. In fact, we have yet to see or hear of a teaching situation we don’t firmly believe can be dramatically improved.
We receive dozens of emails from teachers every week who have put our simple strategies into practice and transformed their class.
You must never give in. You must never back down. You must never decide a student’s fate because of where they grow up, who their parents are, or how poorly they’re behaving in the moment.
